metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of choices that are consistent with the Tallying heuristic on trials where Tallying makes a strict prediction (i.e., one option has more feature-wise wins than the other). The experimental design explicitly pits Tallying against WADD on these trials: Tallying chooses the option with more small wins, whereas WADD chooses the option with a single massive win on a heavily weighted feature. Consequently, data simulated under Tallying will yield a metric value close to 1.0, while data simulated under WADD will yield a value close to 0.0.

Trial 4 and Trial 1 are perfectly opposed for WADD versus Tallying. In Trial 4 (A=[5, 0, 0, 0], B=[0, 1, 1, 1]), WADD strongly prefers A due to the high validity of the first cue and its large magnitude difference, whereas Tallying prefers B because it wins on 3 out of 4 features. In Trial 1 (A=[0, 4, 4, 4], B=[5, 3, 3, 3]), WADD prefers B due to the first cue, while Tallying prefers A because A wins on 3 features. The metric calculates the difference in the probability of choosing A between Trial 4 and Trial 1. WADD predicts a value near +1, while Tallying predicts a value near -1.

This metric calculates the proportion of times a subject's choice aligns with the Tallying heuristic on 'discordant' trials—those where Tallying and Equal Weight make strictly opposing deterministic predictions. Under the Tallying theory, this proportion will be high (close to 1, minus noise/lapses), whereas under the Equal Weight theory, this proportion will be very low (close to 0), since responses would instead align with the Equal Weight predictions. This yields a massive and highly stable gap between the two theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the deterministic prediction of the Equal Weight (EQW) heuristic, specifically on trials where EQW predicts a strict preference (i.e., the sums of magnitudes are not equal). Because the experimental design includes many trials where EQW and Tallying strongly disagree (e.g., one option has a massive single-feature advantage dominating the sum, while the other option wins by small margins on all other features), an EQW agent will score very high (near 1.0) on this metric, whereas a Tallying agent will systematically choose the opposite option and score very low (near 0.0).

This metric calculates the proportion of choices consistent with the Tallying heuristic on the specific trials designed to strongly dissociate the two models. In these trials, one option wins on three low-validity features (0.5 each) while the other option wins on two high-validity features (0.95 and 0.85). Tallying strictly counts feature wins and prefers the option with three wins, whereas Weighted Tallying sums the validities and prefers the option with two high-validity wins. Tallying will score close to 1, while Weighted Tallying will score close to 0.

This metric isolates 'strict conflict' trials where the Weighted Tallying heuristic and the Tallying heuristic predict opposite choices (i.e., one option wins on the simple count of features, but the other wins when features are weighted by their validities). It calculates the proportion of choices on these specific trials that align with the Weighted Tallying prediction. Data generated by Weighted Tallying will yield values close to 1.0 (subject to noise), whereas data generated by Tallying will yield values close to 0.0.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the unweighted Tallying heuristic on trials where Tallying and Weighted Tallying conflict (either they predict opposite outcomes, or Weighted Tallying predicts a tie while Tallying has a strict preference). Under the pure Weighted Tallying heuristic, subjects will almost never choose the Tally-preferred option on strict disagreement trials, and will choose it ~50% on tie trials, resulting in a low score. The Mixture model, however, blends the two strategies, meaning the Tallying score pulls the probability distribution toward the Tally-preferred option, yielding a significantly higher metric value.

In Trial 1, Option A has a single winning feature with a validity of 1.0, while Option B has two winning features with validities of 0.5 each. The pure Weighted Tallying model calculates a perfect tie (1.0 vs 1.0) and thus predicts exactly a 50% chance of choosing Option B (response = 1). The competing Mixture model, however, incorporates a Tallying component that simply counts winning features. Since Option B wins on more features (2 vs 1), the Tallying component strongly prefers B. Consequently, the Mixture model will predict a significantly higher probability of choosing Option B than 0.5. Measuring the mean response on this specific trial isolates this theoretical divergence.

The metric computes the difference in the probability of choosing option A between Trial 1 (where option A has an initial rating of 2) and Trial 3 (where option A has an initial rating of 10). The Mixture model, which relies on tallying wins, strongly prefers A in Trial 1 and B in Trial 3. In contrast, the WADD model, which integrates feature magnitudes, strongly prefers B in Trial 1 and A in Trial 3. This creates a large positive value for the Mixture model and a large negative value for the WADD model, making it highly discriminative.

The metric computes the difference in the rate of choosing Option B across three specific trial types designed to perfectly dissociate the models. In Trial 1, WADD chooses A (response=0) due to the massive magnitude on a highly valid feature, whereas Tallying chooses B (response=1) because B wins on 4 out of 5 features. Conversely, in Trials 2 and 5, WADD chooses B (response=1) due to B's huge magnitude advantage on a single feature, while Tallying chooses A (response=0) because A wins on 4 out of 5 features. By computing `mean(Response_T1) - mean(Response_T2) - mean(Response_T5)`, the WADD model yields values near -2 (0 - 1 - 1), while the Mixture of Tallying model yields values near 1 (1 - 0 - 0). This creates a massive, consistent gap between the theories.
